coredata.dc:description: The use of biodegradable plastic films made of poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) to improve crop production has been proposed. Because the film after use is expected to be degraded on site, it is important to understand the biodegradation mechanism of PBAT in aerobic and mild temperature conditions. We therefore isolated three PBAT-degrading strains, NKCM3201, NKCM3202, and NKCM3101, from soil environments. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that the strains are closely related to Bacillus pumilus. Strain NKCM3201, which degraded PBAT film at the fastest rate (12.2 μg/day/cm2) and grew well at 30 °C to 40 °C in aerobic conditions, was selected for further analysis. We cloned the 648-bp coding region of the PBAT hydrolase (PBATH Bp ) gene, which encodes a 215-amino acid protein containing a signal peptide of 34 residues. Mutation analyses revealed that PBATH Bp belongs to the serine hydrolase superfamily, with a catalytic triad composed of Ser77, Asp133, and His156. Homology 3D modeling of PBATH Bp using Bacillus subtilis 168 lipase as a template showed that the enzyme belongs to the α/β hydrolase fold family, which lack a lid domain on its surface. PBATH Bp hydrolyzed PBAT, poly(butylene succinate-co-adipate) (PBSA), poly(ethylene succinate) (PESu), and polycaprolactone (PCL) films at a degradation rate of 14.3, 3.3 × 102, 7.0 × 102, and 1.1 × 102 μg/cm2/day, respectively. Liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry analysis of degradation products from PBAT revealed that PBATH Bp hydrolyses ester bonds between butanediol and terephthalate (B-T bonds) at much slower rates than ester bonds between adipate and butanediol. This ester bond preference may explain the very slow PBAT degradation rate compared to PBSA, PESu, and PCL. This is the first report of a PBAT hydrolase from an aerobic mesophilic bacterium, and may contribute to our understanding of PBAT biodegradation under mild temperature conditions.

Black bar indicates 0.5% estimated sequence divergences.

Dendrogram of amino acid sequences of PBATH Bp and the homologous proteins. Amino acid sequences of PBATH Bp and the homologous proteins were aligned with program ClustalW. A dendrogram was constructed with MEGA6 on the basis of the alignment data. Black bar indicates 10% estimated sequence divergences (0.1). * It is encoded by a gene that is annotated as a lipase.

Prediction model of PBATH Bp . Model was constructed at SWISS-MODEL (http://swissmodel.expasy.org) using Bacillus subtilis lipase (1i6w.1.A), which shares 81% amino acid sequence identity with PBATH Bp , as a template. Ribbon model of PBATH Bp was depicted in (a) using program VMD 1.9.2. Alpha helix and beta sheet structures were marked with purple and yellow, respectively. Catalytic triad, Ser77, Asp133, and His156, which were determined by mutational analysis, were shown in the model. Space-filling model of PBATH Bp , which was observed from upper site of active site (Ser77 was marked with red), was depicted in (b) using program UCSF chimera. Dashed line shows groove formed in the vicinity of active site. Hydrophobic amino acid residues, which was marked with green, were observed in the vicinity of the active site. ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: The use of biodegradable plastic films made of poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) to improve crop production has been proposed. PBAT hydrolase gene from Bacillus pumilus strain NKCM3201

ce:section.ce:para: The use of plastic mulches improves the quantity and quality of crop production [1]. However, these plastic mulches are made of general polymers scarcely degraded in a natural environment due to their stability and may thus cause economic and environmental problems [2]. Therefore, biodegradable plastic mulches, which allow for onsite disposal, have been pursued as a solution to these problems [2,3].

Poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) is a biodegradable aliphatic-aromatic copolyester produced by BASF under the trade name of Ecoflex. PBAT is used in biodegradable mulch film due to good mechanical and thermal properties and good film formability [4–6]. PBAT-degrading thermophilic microorganisms from compost have been characterized in studies of the biodegradation mechanism [7,8]. In compost, a thermophilic actinomycete, Thermobifida fusca K13 g, has been found to play an important role in the degradation of PBAT even though the strain alone cannot mineralize it [7,8]. Eventually, PBAT degradation products are completely mineralized by symbionts [8]. In addition, characterization of PBAT hydrolase from T. fusca revealed that the enzyme is a cutinase [9,10], which degrades the plant polyester cutin. PBAT hydrolases from other thermophilic microorganisms such as Thermobifida alba, Saccharomonospora viridis, Thermobifida cellulosilytica, and Humicola insolens are also cutinases [11–13]. Crystal structure analysis of the PBAT hydrolase from the T. alba strain AHK119 showed that the enzyme belongs to the α/β hydrolase family, whose members lack a lid domain [14].

Because PBAT is used as mulch film in a natural environment, understanding PBAT-degrading mesophiles is important in the context of onsite degradation [15,16]. In a previous study, we revealed that the mesophilic fungus Isaria fumosorosea strain NKCM1712 contributes to the degradation and mineralization of PBAT in natural environments [15]. In addition, Paraphoma-related fungus cutinase-like enzyme (PCLE) and Cryptococcus flavus cutinase-like enzyme (CfCLE) can degrade PBAT under mild conditions [17,18]. It has been reported that mesophilic bacteria also contribute to PBAT degradation under mild conditions [16]. Recent studies showed that two PBAT hydrolases from the anaerobic mesophilic bacteria Pelosinus fermentans and Clostridium botulinum are α/β hydrolases with a lid domain [19,20]. In contrast, to our knowledge, no PBAT hydrolases from aerobic mesophilic bacteria have been reported. Because biodegradable mulch film is degraded in aerobic conditions in natural environments, it is important to characterize PBAT hydrolases from these bacteria. We have therefore characterized the first PBAT hydrolase from an aerobic mesophilic PBAT-degrading bacterium isolated from a natural environment.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Isolation and identification of PBAT-degrading microorganisms
ce:section.ce:para: Clear zone method was used for isolation of PBAT-degrading microorganisms [15]. Each 1 g of soils, corresponding to andosol and gravelly soils collected from 2 fields (Shibukawa, Gunma, Japan: 36°31′55.952″N, 139°0′40.013″E, and Nanjo, Okinawa, Japan: 26°8′31.8″N, 127°44′57.7″E, respectively) was suspended in 10 mL of distilled water, and the suspension was stood for 10 min. After 100 μL of supernatants were plated onto PBAT-containing plate (4.6 g/L of KH2PO4, 11.6 g/L of Na2HPO4·12H2O, 1.0 g/L of NH4Cl, 0.5 g/L of MgSO4·7H2O, 0.1 g/L of FeCl3·6H2O, 0.5 g/L of dried yeast extract (Nihon Pharmaceutical), 0.1 g/L of Plysurf, 0.2% (w/v) of emulsified PBAT, and 1.5% (w/v) of agar, pH 7.0) [15], the plate was incubated at 30 °C. Bacteria that formed clear zone on the plate were opted as PBAT-degrading bacteria and further purified on solid LB media (5 g/L of NaCl, 10 g/L of polypeptone (Nihon Pharmaceutical), 5 g/L of dried yeast extract (Nihon Pharmaceutical), and 1.5% (w/v) of agar, pH 7.5) [15] by streak culture. To identify PBAT-degrading bacteria, phylogenetic analysis was performed on the basis of its 16S rDNA sequence amplified with polymerase chain reaction (PCR) previously described [21]. Amplified DNA were ligated into pMD20 and sequenced by dideoxy method (Eurofins Genomics K.K.). The sequences were compared with GenBank data using program nucleotide BLAST at NCBI (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov) to search the related species. Multiple sequence alignment was performed with program ClustalW at DNA databank of Japan (DDBJ) (http://clustalw.ddbj.nig.ac.jp). Then, phylogenetic trees were constructed with MEGA6 [22] using the neighbor-joining method [23].

ce:section.ce:section-title: Ability of PBAT-degrading isolates to degrade 7 polyesters
ce:section.ce:para: Three PBAT-degrading bacterial isolates were plated on 7 emulsified polyesters-containing plates (PBAT, PCL, PBSu, PBSA, PESu, PHB, and PLA). These plates were incubated at 30 °C for 2 weeks. The clear zone formation by these strains was confirmed.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Ability of PBAT-degrading isolates to degrade PBAT film
ce:section.ce:para: To investigate their ability to degrade PBAT film, these bacteria were cultured in 3 mL of liquid basal medium (4.6 g/L of KH2PO4, 11.6 g/L of Na2HPO4·12H2O, 1.0 g/L of NH4Cl, 0.5 g/L of MgSO4·7H2O, 0.1 g/L of FeCl3·6H2O, 0.5 g/L of dried yeast extract, pH 7.0) containing melt-pressed PBAT film (1 cm × 1 cm × 0.1 mm) at 30 °C for 10 days under shaking culture condition (120 strokes per minute). The film was recovered from culture medium, and then washed with methanol and distilled water. They were dried in vacuo for 1 day, and their dry weights were measured (n = 5).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Characterization of a PBAT-degrading isolate, strain NKCM3201
ce:section.ce:para: Effect of temperature on growth of strain NKCM3201 was investigated. Strain NKCM3201 was incubated on PBAT-containing plate at 4, 20, 25, 30, 37, 40, or 50 °C. Colony and clear zone formation were confirmed. Physiological and biochemical properties of the strain were investigated using API 20NE and API ZYM (bioMériux) as previously described [21]. Whether, or not the strain use PBAT monomer(terephthalic acid, adipic acid, and 1,4-butanediol)s were investigated. The strain was cultured in liquid basal medium supplemented with each 0.2% (w/v) of 1,4-butene diol, adipic acid, or terephthalic acid at 30 °C under shaking condition (120 strokes/minute). As a control, the strain was cultured in liquid basal medium without PBAT monomers. The abilities were evaluated by optical densities measurement of these cultures at 600 nm after incubation for 24 h.

PBAT hydrolase (PBATH Bp ) gene (pbath
Bp ) was cloned from the isolate, strain NKCM3201. Extraction of genomic DNA (gDNA) from the strain was performed as previously described [21]. To amplify pbath
Bp using PCR method, 4 primers (Dep1, Dep2, Dep3, and Dep4; Table 2, Fig. S1-a) were designed on the basis of genome sequence from B. pumilus strain SAFR-032 (Locus: CP000813, BPUM_2613) and lipase gene from B. licheniformis (Accession: CAB95850). An ORF of triacylglycerol lipase gene was amplified using primers Dep1 and Dep2 (Table 2, Fig. S1-a), gDNA, and TaKaRa Ex Taq according to manufacturer's instructions (Takara Bio). Amplified DNA was sequenced as described in section 2.2. Two primers, Dep5 and Dep6, were designed on the basis of the cloned DNA sequence to amplify upstream and downstream regions of the ORF. Amplification of upstream and downstream regions was performed using primers Dep3 and Dep5, and primers Dep4 and Dep6, respectively. A DNA fragment that contains the ORF and its upstream and downstream regions was amplified with Dep7 and Dep8, which designed on the basis of the cloned upstream and downstream DNA sequences (Fig. S1-a). Thermal cycles used in the PCR are listed in Table S1. The amplified DNA was ligated into pMD20 (the resulting plasmid was denoted as pMDLP) (Table 1
, Fig. S1-a). PBAT hydrolytic activity by recombinant Escherichia coli DH5α-carrying pMDLP was confirmed by clear zone formation on the PBAT-containing plate at 37 °C.

Heterologous expression system of PBATH Bp was constructed in Brevibacillus choshinensis SP3 (Takara Bio). PCR primers BrlipF and BrlipR (Table 2) containing restriction sites Pst I and EcoR I, respectively, were designed to amplify a gene encoding PBATH Bp excluding its deduced signal peptide sequence, which was deduced with SignalP 4.1 server (see section 2.7). The gene was amplified using PrimeSTAR® DNA polymerase according to the manufacturer's instructions (Takara Bio). Thermal cycles were listed in Table S1. PCR product digested by Pst I and EcoR I was ligated to the Pst I and EcoR I restriction sites that are located downstream of the signal peptide [34] of a shuttle vector, pNCMO2 (Table 1, Fig. S1-(b)), resulting in recombinant plasmid DNA (pNCLP). pNCLP was introduced into B. choshinensis SP3 by electroporation, according to the manufacturer's instructions (Takara Bio). The transformant that secretes a PBATH Bp (B. choshinensis PBATH; Table 1) was opted on the PBAT containing solid LB medium with clear zone method.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Amino acid sequence analysis and homology modeling of PBATHBp
ce:section.ce:para: Amino acid sequence of PBATH Bp from NKCM3201 was deduced with GENETYX-MAC Ver.16 (GENETYX). Signal peptide was deduced using SignalP 4.1 server (http://www.cbs.dtu.dk/services/SignalP/). Dendrogram of the hydrolase and homologous proteins was constructed with MEGA6 [22] after the sequences were aligned with program ClustalW (http://clustalw.ddbj.nig.ac.jp). Homology model of PBATH Bp was generated using a datum of Bacillus subtilis lipase A whose amino acid sequence shared 81% homology with that of PBATH Bp as a template (1i6w) at SWISS-MODEL (https://swissmodel.expasy.org) [24]. The model was depicted with VMD 1.9.2 [25] and UCSF Chimera [26].

To determine catalytic triad of PBATH Bp , the deduced 3 catalytic residues; Ser77, Asp133, and His156 were substituted to Ala, Asn, and Asn, respectively. Three mutated genes, designated as S77A, D133 N, and H156 N were prepared by overlap PCR method using mutagenic primers (Table 2) [27]. PCR mixture was as follows: gDNA (300 ng), 5 × PrimeSTAR buffer (Mg2+ plus) (4.0 μL), dNTP mixture (2.5 mM each; 1.6 μL), primer pairs (BrlipF and S77A-R, BrlipR and S77A-F for construction of S77A), (BrlipF and D133N-R, BrlipR and D133N-F for construction of D133 N), (BrlipF and H156N-R, and BrlipR and H156N-F for construction of H156 N) (each 10 pmol), and PrimeSTAR HS DNA polymerase (0.25 U) (Takara Bio Inc.). Thermal cycles were as follows: 1 cycle of 98 °C for 3 min, 25 cycles of 98 °C for 30 s, 55 °C for 15 s, and 72 °C for 1 min, and 1 cycle of 72 °C for 5 min. To ligate each pair of DNA fragments, overlap PCR was performed. PCR mixtures were as follows: each DNA fragment (1.0 μL), 5 × PrimeSTAR Buffer (Mg2+ plus) (4.0 μL), dNTP Mixture (2.5 mM each; 1.6 μL), PrimeSTAR DNA polymerase (0.25 U), and ddH2O (up to 18 μL). Thermal cycles were as follows: 1 cycle of 98 °C for 3 min, 5 cycles of 98 °C for 30 s and 68 °C for 1 min. After primers, BrlipF and BrlipR (each 1.0 μL), were added to the mixture, PCR to amplify the ligated DNA was performed as follows: 1 cycle of 98 °C for 3 min, 25 cycles of 98 °C for 30 s and 68 °C for 1 min. Amplified DNAs were ligated into pNCMO2 to construct pNCLP-S77A, pNCLP-D133 N, and pNCLP-H156 N (Table 2). Mutated genes were confirmed by DNA sequencing. The activities of mutated enzymes that were produced by the recombinants respectively, were evaluated with clear zone method on PBAT-containing plate by streak culture of the recombinants.

PBATH Bp -expressing transformant, B. choshinensis PBATH (Table 1), was aerobically incubated in 500 mL of LB medium at 37 °C for 24 h under shaking culture condition (120 strokes/minute). By centrifugation of the culture, culture supernatant was recovered. Crude enzyme of PBATH Bp was recovered with centrifugation at 8000 rpm at 4 °C for 15 min as precipitate at 60% ammonium sulfate saturation. It was dissolved in 5 mL of 10 mM phosphate buffer (pH 7.0). After the fraction was dialyzed in 1 L of 10 mM phosphate buffer, it was concentrated to 2 mL using a water-absorbable polymer that was made from crosslinking sodium polyacrylate, AQUA KEEP (Sumitomo Seika Chemicals Co., Ltd.). Crude enzyme was further purified by a gel filtration with HiLoad ™ 16/60 Superdex ™ 75 prep grade column (GE Healthcare Japan Co.) at 0.8 mL/min of flow rate using 10 mM phosphate buffer containing 250 mM NaCl as mobile phase at 4 °C. Fractions that possessed p-nitrophenyl acetate (PNPA) hydrolytic activity were collected and dialyzed in 1 L of 10 mM phosphate buffer. Sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) was performed using Laemmli method to confirm the purity [28]. Protein was stained with a CBB staining kit (Rapid CBB KANTO, Kanto Chemical). Protein was determined by Bradford protein assay [29].

To investigate hydrolytic activities of PBATH Bp toward six para-nitrophenyl esters substrates: p-nitrophenyl acetate (PNPA), p-nitrophenyl butyrate (PNPB), p-nitrophenyl caprylate (PNPC), p-nitrophenyl laurate (PNPL), p-nitrophenyl myristate (PNPM), and p-nitrophenyl palmitate (PNPP), absorbance changes at 405 nm of wavelength of reaction mixtures of 1 mL: 0.53 μg of PBATH Bp , 100 μL of substrate solutions (1 mg of the substrates, 49.5 μL of 1,4-dioxane and 49.5 μL of nonaethylene glycol monododecyl ether), and 900 μL of 50 mM phosphate buffer (pH 7.0), were monitored at 30 °C for 30 min. One unit was defined as the activity of the enzyme that hydrolyze 1 μmol of p-nitrophenyl ester for 1 min at 30 °C in the buffer. Mole number of p-nitrophenol was calculated with Beer-Lambert law (absorbance = εcl, ε: extinction coefficient, 1.85 × 104 l mol−1 cm−1, c: concentration of substrate, l: cell length).

To investigate thermal stability, 0.53 μg of PBATH Bp was incubated at 4, 10, 20, 30, 40, 45, 50, or 60 °C for 30 min. To investigate pH stability, 0.53 μg of PBATH Bp was incubated in several buffers (pH 2.0 to 10.5) at 30 °C for 5 h. Residual activities were determined using substrate solution containing PNPA.

Effects of chemicals and metals on enzyme activity were also analyzed. Zero point five three μg of PBATH Bp was incubated with 5 chemicals: phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF), diisopropyl fluorophosphonate (DFP), diazoacetyl-D,l-norleucine methyl ester (DAN), dithiothreitol (DTT), and ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), at final concentrations of 0.2, 0.2, 1.0, 5.0, and 10 mM, respectively, for 30 min at 30 °C. In addition, 0.53 μg of PBATH Bp was incubated with 1 and 2 mol equivalent numbers of the metal ions (KCl, MgCl2, CaCl2, CaCl2 plus EDTA, FeCl2, MnCl2, and ZnCl2) for 5 min at 30 °C. Effects of chemicals and metals on the enzyme were evaluated by residual activities determination using PNPA.

Lipase activity of PBATH Bp was determined using the clear zone method [9]. One point eight microgram of PBATH Bp was dropped on emulsified olive oil-containing plate (0.2% olive oil emulsion, 50 mM KH2PO4, 1.5% (w/v) of agar, pH 7.0) and incubated at 30 °C for 24 h. Lipase activity was evaluated based on the appearance of the clear zone.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Degradation of PBAT and other polyester films by PBATHBp
ce:section.ce:para: Polyesters [PBAT, PCL, PESu, and P(3HB)] films were put into 1 ml of 50 mM phosphate buffer solution (pH 7.0) containing 3.5 μg of PBATH Bp in 10 mL glass vials, respectively (n = 5). As a control, the films were put into 1 ml of the solution without PBATH Bp (n = 5). They were incubated at 30 °C for several days. The films were collected and washed with methanol and distilled water. After they were dried in vacuo, their weights were determined. Degradation rate (mg/cm2/day) was calculated by dividing the amount of weight loss (mg) by apparent surface area of the film (cm2) and incubation time (day). Molecular masses of the films were analyzed by gel permeation chromatography (GPC) using HLC-8220GPC with 3 columns (TSKgelGMHXL, TSKgelG1000HXL, TSKgelG2000HXL) (Tosoh Corporation). Chloroform was used as mobile phase at the flow rate of 1.0 mL/min at 40 °C. Polystyrene standards were used to generate a calibration curve. Surface morphology of PBAT film, which was coated with Au-Pd using Magnetron Sputter MSP-1S (Vacuum Device Inc.), was observed with scanning electron microscopy (SEM: SSX-550, Shimadzu Co., Ltd.) under high vacuum conditions at 15 kV of accelerating voltage.

Three PBAT films were incubated in the 1 ml of phosphate buffer with 7.0 μg of PBATH Bp at 30 °C for 2 days. The degradation products were identified using liquid chromatography mass spectrometry (LC/MS). Acetonitrile/0.1% formic acid solution(30/70, v/v) (Solution A) and acetonitrile (Solution B) were used as mobile phase. InertSustain™ C18 column (2.1 × 150 mm) (GL Science) was used as stationary phase. Degradation products were separated by gradient system by HPLC using Waters 1515 Isocratic HPLC Pump (Waters) at the flow rate of 0.2 mL/min at 40 °C of column temperature. Solvent gradient was as follows: 0–10 min, 100% Solution A; 10–20 min, 0–100% Solution B, linear gradient; 20–30 min, 100% Solution B. Detection of the products was performed with Waters 2487 Dual λ Absorbance Detector at the wavelength of 254 nm. The products were identified with Waters micromass ZQ. MS condition was as follows: capillary voltage 2.5 kV; cone voltage 20 kV; source temperature 120 °C; desolvation temperature 350 °C; cone gas flow 50 L/h; desolvation gas flow 350 L/h. Bis(4-hydroxybutyl) terephthalate (BTB), which did not detect by MS, was identified by comparing HPLC chart of sample with that of BTB as a standard. which was synthesized from terephthalic acid and 1,4-butanediol [30]. Concentrated sulfuric acid (100 μL, 0.55 mmol) was added to a mixture of terephthalic acid (890 mg, 5.0 mmol) and 1,4-butanediol (10.0 mL, 112 mmol). The solution was stirred at 100 °C for 15 h. After cooling to room temperature, the solution was based with 5% sodium carbonate solution and extracted with ethyl acetate. The organic layer was washed with water and brine, dried with anhydrous magnesium sulfate, and evaporated in vacuo to give 996 mg (64%) of bis(4-hydroxybutyl)terephthalate as white solid. (1H NMR (400 MHz, CDCl3), δ 8.12 (4H, s), 4.41 (4H, t, J = 6.8 Hz), 3.76 (4H, t, J = 6.8 Hz), 1.95–1.88 (4H, m), 1.79–1.73 (4H, m), 1.45 (2H, brs) ppm.) Quantification of degradation products containing aromatic ring was HPLC with LC-2000Plus series (PU-2080 Plus; LG-2080; AS-2051 Plus; CO-2060 Plus; UV-2075 Plus, JASCO Corporation) using the known concentration of terephthalic acid as a standard.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Ability of PBATHBp to degrade degradation products of PBAT
ce:section.ce:para: Three PBAT films were incubated in the 1 ml of phosphate buffer with 7.0 μg of PBATH Bp at 30 °C for 2 days. After 3.5 μg of PBATH Bp was added to 500 μL of the supernatant, the solution was incubated at 30 °C. Degradation products were determined by HPLC as previously described in section 2.12.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Isolation and characterization of PBAT-degrading bacteria
ce:section.ce:para: We have isolated three PBAT-degrading bacteria from two field soils by the clear-zone method. The isolates were designated as strains NKCM3101, NKCM3201, and NKCM3202. Fig. 2 shows a phylogenetic tree of these isolates and related species based on 16S rDNA sequence. Strains NKCM3101, NKCM3201, and NKCM3202 are closely related to Bacillus pumilus that belongs to the phylum Firmicutes.

The three isolates did not form clear zones on plates containing P(3HB) and PLA, but did form clear zones in plates containing PBSA, PBSu, PCL, and PESu in addition to PBAT (Table 3 ). The isolates could also degrade solid PBAT film (Table 3). On the other hand, B. pumilus KT1012, previously isolated in our laboratory, could not form clear zones on PBAT-containing plates. Among the three isolates, strain NKCM3201 showed the highest PBAT film degradation activity (12.2 μg/day/cm2), and was therefore further characterized in detail. The strain grew well from 30 °C to 40 °C, and could form large clear zones from 30 °C to 37 °C. The strain hardly metabolized all PBAT constituents: 1,4-butanediol, adipic acid, and terephthalic acid, during 24 h at 30 °C. The physiological and biochemical properties of the strain are shown in Tables S2 and S3.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Cloning of the PBAT hydrolase gene from strain NKCM3201
ce:section.ce:para: The higher order structure of the PBAT hydrolase from Thermobifida alba AHK119 showed that the enzyme is a cutinase, namely, a lipase lacking a lid domain. We therefore focused on lipases with this characteristic to identify and clone an orthologous gene from B. pumilus NKCM3201 gDNA. We found one gene (locus: BPUM_2613) encoding a lipase (EC number: 3.1.1.3) in the B. pumilus SAFR-032 genome sequence with 80% identity to Bacillus subtilis lipase without a lid domain (LipA). Primers were then designed based on this gene sequence to amplify the gene of a PBAT hydrolase from B. pumilus NKCM3201.

DNA amplified by PCR using primers targeting the putative PBAT hydrolase gene was cloned into pMD20, yielding plasmid pMDLP (Table 1). E. coli harboring pMDLP (E. coli PBATH) formed clear zones on PBAT-containing plates. In addition, B. choshinensis SP3 harboring pNCLP also formed a clear zone on the plate. These results indicate that the pbath
Bp gene product confers PBAT hydrolytic ability to these host strains. Fig. S2 shows the sequence of the cloned DNA. The 1289-base pair (bp) DNA contained a 648-bp triacylglycerol lipase gene, which was designated as PBAT hydrolase (PBATH Bp ) gene (pbath
Bp ). The open reading frame (ORF) of PBATH Bp encoded a protein of 215 amino acid residues with 81% identity to LipA. Thirty-four amino acids were identified as a signal peptide sequence using program SignalP 4.1 Server. The molecular mass of the mature protein was estimated to be 19.2 kDa. Based on the comparison of PBATH Bp and LipA amino acid sequences, residues Ser77, Asp133, and His156 were predicted as a catalytic triad. The consensus motif A-X-S-X-G was also observed in the PBATH Bp amino acid sequence (Fig. S2).

Fig. 3 shows a dendrogram constructed with the amino acid sequence of several hydrolases. PBATH Bp exhibited no significant sequence similarity with microbial enzymes that have the ability to degrade PBAT (BTA1 (CAH17553), BTA2 (CAH17554), Est1 [36], Est119 [11], Cbotu_EstA [20], Cbotu_EstB [20], PCLE [17], and PfL1 [19]), whereas it showed a high degree of similarity with Paenibacillus amylolyticus poly(dl-lactic acid) depolymerase (PlaA) [31], LipA [32], and B. licheniformis lipases [33] (51, 81, and 97% identity, respectively).

The predicted 3D model of PBATH Bp was generated using B. subtilis lipase LipA structure as a template. The resulting ribbon and space-filling representations of the model are shown in Fig. 4 . PBATH Bp belongs to the α/β hydrolase fold family, and has five α-helices and a six-stranded β-sheet. The model shows that PBATH Bp lacks a lid domain, and that the deduced catalytic triad Ser77, Asn133, and His156 is present at the surface of PBATH Bp (Fig. 4a). In addition, grooves described as accommodating the aliphatic chain of lipids [32] are found in the vicinity of the active site (Fig. 4b). The grooves contain the hydrophobic amino acid residues Ile12, Met78, Leu108, Leu134, Ile135, Val136, Val137, Leu140, Ile157, and Leu160, all marked in green (Fig. 4b).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Mutational analysis of the predicted catalytic triad of PBATH Bp
ce:section.ce:para: To determine the catalytic triad of PBATH Bp , residues Ser77, Asp133, and His156, tentatively identified as the catalytic triad, were mutated to Ala77, Asn133, and Asn156, respectively. The B. choshinensis strains S77A, D133 N, and H156 N, which expressed the mutated proteins, were cultured on PBAT-containing plates at 30 °C. All three strains lacked the ability to degrade the five polyesters (including PBAT) used in this study (Table 3). We conclude that residues Ser77, Asn133, and His156 are essential for the catalytic activity of PBATH Bp .

To obtain purified PBATH Bp for enzymatic characterization, we used the Brevibacillus expression system, which has been successfully used for secretory production of heterologous proteins [34]. DNA sequence encoding the predicted mature PBATH Bp was cloned into restriction sites (Pst I and EcoR I) of pNCMO2, and was designated as pNCLP (Table 1). B. choshinensis harboring pNCLP (B. choshinensis PBATH) secreted PBATH Bp enzyme, which was purified from the culture supernatant by ammonium precipitation and gel filtration chromatography. Fig. S3 shows the elution profile of PBATH Bp in the gel filtration chromatography, and fractions containing PNPA hydrolytic activity were collected. Table 4 summarizes the purification steps to obtain PBATH Bp . SDS-PAGE analysis of the purified fractions shows a single polypeptide with apparent molecular weight of approximately 19 kDa (Fig. 5 , lane 3), based on which we considered PBATH Bp to be purified to homogeneity.

The effects of temperature and pH on PBATH Bp enzymatic activity were determined. The residual activities of the enzyme incubated at 4 °C, 10 °C, 20 °C, 30 °C, and 40 °C for 30 min were stable, whereas the activity at 45 °C showed a decreased of about 92% (Fig. S4). In addition, activity was completely lost after incubation at 50 °C and 60 °C. PBATH Bp enzymatic activity in the pH range of 6.0–10.5 was stable, whereas the activity was lost at low pH (2.0–4.0) (Fig. S5).

The effects of several chemicals on PBATH Bp hydrolytic activity were also investigated. DAN, EDTA, and DTT showed little effect on enzymatic activity (92%, 99%, and 100% of residual activities, respectively). On the other hand, DFP and PMSF decreased the activity by 7% and 3%, respectively. Two metal ions, added as KCl and ZnCl2, hardly affected PBATH Bp activity (88% and 90% of residual activities, respectively), whereas the activity decreased by 82%, 68%, and 73% when the enzyme was incubated with twice the amount of MgCl2, FeCl2, and MnCl2, respectively. In contrast, PBATH Bp activity increased by 113% in the presence of CaCl2, although the activity was unchanged in the presence of equal amounts of both CaCl2 and EDTA (Table 5 ).

The substrate specificity of PBATH Bp was investigated using p-nitrophenyl esters as substrates of the enzyme. Fig. 6 shows the hydrolytic activity of PBATH Bp on several p-nitrophenyl esters at 30 °C. PBATH Bp showed the highest hydrolytic activity on PNPA, which has the shortest carbon chain length (C = 2). The hydrolytic activity was reduced with the increase in carbon chain length of p-nitrophenyl esters, such that the hydrolytic activities on PNPL, PNPM, and PNPP were 19 times lower than that on PNPA. In addition, PBATH Bp formed a clear zone on olive oil-containing plates after incubation at 30 °C for 24 h, indicating that the enzyme has lipase activity (Fig. S6).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Degradation of PBAT and other polyester films by PBATHBp
ce:section.ce:para: The ability of PBATH Bp to degrade PBAT film was investigated in terms of film weight loss (Fig. 7 a). The observed degradation rate was 14.3 μg/cm2/day. However, the molecular weight of PBAT films did not change significantly before and after incubation with PBATH Bp (Table S4). SEM images showed that film surfaces before and after incubation in buffer without PBATH Bp were smooth (Fig. 7b-1 and b-2), whereas some cracks were observed on film surfaces after incubation with PBATH Bp (Fig. 7b-3).

The ability of PBATH Bp to degrade four other polyester films, PBSA, PESu, PCL, and P(3HB), was also investigated (Fig. 7a). PBATH Bp was unable to degrade bacterial polyester P(3HB), but degraded PBSA, PESu, and PCL films at a rate of 3.3 × 102, 7.0 × 102, and 1.1 × 102 μg/cm2/day, respectively. These degradation rates were much faster compared to that of PBAT. The molecular weight of these polyesters hardly changed before and after incubation in phosphate buffer solution with PBATH Bp (Table S4).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Identification and quantification of PBAT degradation products by PBATHBp
ce:section.ce:para: To identify the degradation products of PBAT digested by PBATH Bp , enzymatic hydrolysates of PBAT film were analyzed after incubation at 30 °C for 48 h (Fig. S7). Terephthalic acid (T), adipic acid (A), 1,4-butanediol (B), AB, TB, ABA, BTB, ABT, BABT (BABT or BTBA), ABABA, and ABABT (ABABT or ABTBA) were detected by ESI-MS as degradation products (Fig. S8). In addition, the products with aromatic rings were determined by HPLC with a UV detector at 254 nm. The concentration of T, TB, BTB, ABT, BTBA (BTBA or BABT), and ABABT (ABABT or ABTBA) were 3.0, 50, 50, 18, 59, and 13 nmol/μL, respectively (Fig. 7c, grey bars). After the film was removed from the reaction mixture, PBATH Bp was added, and then the mixture was further incubated at 30 °C for 22 h. The contents of ABT, BABT (BABT or BTBA), and ABTBA (ABABT or ABABT) decreased (5.4, 5.7, and 0 nmol/μL, respectively), whereas those of T, BT, and BTB increased (9.8, 121, and 58 nmol/μL, respectively) compared to those before incubation (Fig. 7c, striped bars). These results are consistent with the B-T bond being less easily cleaved than the A-B bond by PBATH Bp .

The PBAT biodegradation mechanism under high temperature conditions has been investigated in detail [5–9,11–14,35–37], whereas the mechanism in mild conditions is poorly understood [15–21,38]. In particular, PBAT hydrolases produced by aerobic mesophilic PBAT-degrading bacteria has never been reported. However, considering that PBAT could be widely used in agricultural materials, it is important to understand the PBAT biodegradation mechanism under mild conditions. Therefore, we have isolated aerobic mesophilic bacteria and cloned and characterized the corresponding PBAT hydrolase.

Three PBAT degrading-bacteria (strains NKCM3201, NKCM3202, and NKCM3101) described in this study are closely related to Bacillus pumilus that belongs to the phylum Firmicutes, which is commonly found in soil environments [39–41]. Because strain NKCM3201 showed the highest activity in PBAT film degradation, the strain was further characterized in detail. Strain NKCM3201 is a typical aerobic mesophile, with a relatively high growth rate at 30 °C to 40 °C, and was unable to metabolize PBAT monomers, despite the fact that PBATH Bp isolated from this strain hydrolyzed PBAT into hydrolytic oligomers and monomers. The strain also degraded PESu, PBSA, PBSu, and PCL at mild conditions. To begin characterization of the enzyme responsible for degrading PBAT in strain NKCM3201, we cloned the corresponding gene.

Two types of transformants harboring pbath
Bp (E. coli PBATH and B. choshinensis PBATH) degraded PBAT, suggesting that pbath
Bp is one of the genes responsible for PBAT hydrolytic activity in the NKCM3201 strain. PBATH Bp is closely related to B. subtilis lipase (LipA) and B. licheniformis lipase (Fig. 3), indicating that the enzyme belongs to the lipase family I.4, which is a group of lipases with small molecular mass. PBATH Bp was predicted to have a serine residue in the active site, because it is sensitive to typical serine hydrolase inhibitors such as DFP and PMSF. In addition, mutation analyses revealed that the catalytic triad of PBATH Bp is composed of Ser77, Asp133, and His156. Homology 3D modeling showed that PBATH Bp does not possess a lid domain to cover its hydrophobic pocket. Similarly, other polyester-degrading enzymes such as cutinases and P(3HB) depolymerases [14,42,43] lack lid domains. In general, the lid domain found in many lipases functions not at solid-liquid but at liquid-liquid interfaces to increase activity. Because lid domains are unnecessary in solid-liquid interfaces, it is unsurprising that polyester-degrading enzymes, including PBATH Bp , lack these structures. On the contrary, lack of the lid domain would be advantageous for degrading solid polyesters because the substrate would be more easily accommodated in the active site of these enzymes [44].

PBATH Bp exhibited broad substrate specificity for the biodegradable polyesters PBAT, PBSA, PBSu, PCL, and PESu (Table 3 and Fig. 7a). Such broad substrate specificity may be due to substrate recognition through hydrophobic interaction between the polyester substrates and the grooves containing hydrophobic residues in PBATH Bp (Fig. 4) [45]. In addition, PBATH Bp does not hydrolyze P(3HB) or PLA, suggesting that these polyesters are unsuitable as substrates because of the presence of side chains in P(3HB) and PLA [46].

Our results show that PBATH Bp is a mesophilic and alkalophilic enzyme (Figs. S4 and S5). Calcium ion at equimolar amounts to PBATH Bp brought about a 1.12-fold increase in PNPA hydrolytic activity, and the addition of EDTA decreased enzymatic activity to levels similar to those without calcium (Table 5). These results suggest that calcium may regulate PBATH Bp
[12,47].

PBATH Bp showed a preference for short and medium chain para-nitrophenyl esters as substrates: PNPA, PNPB, and PNPC (Fig. 6). In addition, PBATH Bp degraded solid-state substrates (Fig. 7). Considering that general cutinases, which degrade solid-state polyesters, also show high hydrolytic activity for short and medium chain length para-nitrophenyl esters [48,49], PBATH Bp may be more appropriately classified as a cutinase than a lipase.

Weight loss and SEM analysis of PBAT film also demonstrate that PBATH Bp degrades PBAT film (Fig. 7a and b). On the other hand, the molecular mass of the film incubated with PBATH Bp did not change (Table S4), suggesting that degradation during the relatively short incubation time occurred via surface hydrolysis and not by bulk hydrolysis.

Analysis of PBAT degradation products generated by PBATH Bp revealed that monomers and oligomers were released. Further degradation of oligomers containing aromatic rings was monitored (Fig. 7c), and results showed that the content of oligomers containing adipate, butanediol, and A-B bonds decreased, whereas the contents of oligomers containing only butanediol, terephthalate, and B-T bonds increased despite the fact that only small amounts of T accumulated. These results suggest that the B-T bond is less easily cleaved than the A-B bond by PBATH Bp . This preference for A-B bonds rather than B-T bonds is similar to that of other aliphatic-aromatic copolyester-degrading enzymes such as HiC and Cbotu_EstA [13,20]. Our results show that the PBAT degradation rate by PBATH Bp was the slowest compared to that of other polyesters films such as PBSA, PCL, and PESu, which lack aromatic rings in their structure. Similarly, enzymes showing PBAT-degrading activity, such as Est1 [36], PCLE [17], and CfCLE [18], have a much higher hydrolytic activity on aliphatic polyesters compared to PBAT. Such a slow degradation rate of PBAT by PBAT hydrolases including PBATH Bp , might be due to the presence of B-T ester bonds.

In natural environments, PBAT are degraded via various mechanisms: physical, chemical, and biological reactions that include oxidative degradation and hydrolysis [3,15,50]. In this study, we have shown that PBATH Bp from B. pumilus strain NKCM3201 hydrolyzes PBAT, although the strain does not metabolize PBAT monomers. This suggests that the strain is capable of PBAT hydrolytic processes only. On the other hand, considering that PBAT monomers are mineralized in natural environments [51], complete degradation of PBAT in these environments would be achieved by a combination of the NKCM3201 strain and microbial symbionts.
In summary, this is the first report of a PBAT hydrolase from an aerobic mesophilic bacterium, and may contribute to our understanding of PBAT biodegradation under mild temperature conditions.
